Aerial Wildlife Survey Report 
Wildlife Management Unit 102 Aerial Ungulate Survey (2025) 
Background 
Alberta Wildlife Management Unit (WMU) 102 
(Pakowki WMU) is south of Medicine Hat in the 
extreme southeast corner of Alberta.  This WMU 
covers an area of approximately 3177 km2.  WMU 102 
is within Alberta’s dry mixed-grass natural subregion. 
Land is a mixture of deeded and crown land under 
grazing disposition. General habitat and land use 
consists of cultivated cropland for the purpose of 
annual crop production, and tame and native 
grassland used for cattle grazing. The eastern half of 
WMU 102 is primarily large blocks of crown owned 
native grassland including two provincial grazing 
reserves. The Milk River valley is a prominent feature 
angling east and south through the west half of the 
WMU until it enters the USA. This valley includes 
numerous complex and steep coulees as well as 
sagebrush flats and riparian cottonwood forests in the 
valley bottom. Additional significant topographic 
features in the WMU include the Lost River valley, 
Sage Creek valley, and Cutbank Creek valley. Oil and 
gas development is present in some locations in the 
WMU. Chronic Wasting disease is established within 
the WMU, with the highest detected rate of prevalence 
in mule deer being 5.7% in 2021. Submitted samples 
showed prevalence rates of 10.2% in bucks and 2.4% 
in does in that year. 
A survey for ungulates (mule deer, white-tailed deer, 
elk and moose) was last conducted for WMU 102 in 
2018 using the strip transect methodology (Table 1). 
With five years since the last survey, an updated 
population estimate is needed to ensure management 
goals are based on more relevant data.  
The objective of the February 2025 survey was to 
assess the status of the ungulate population in WMU 
102 by determining estimates for abundance, density 
and age-sex composition. We also recorded 
observations of additional species of game 
management or conservation concern including 
pronghorn, carnivores, game birds, and sensitive or at-
risk species. 
S
urvey Method 
A rotary wing (Astar-B3) transect survey was 
conducted February 8 - 9, 2025 flying 33 east-west 
lines at 1.85 km intervals, with 50% coverage (800 m 
wide survey strip, area surveyed 1580.91 km2) for a 
total linear survey effort of 1976 km. At each 
observation point, ungulates were classified by 
species, and when possible, sex and age were 
recorded. Antler size for deer was classified as ‘small’ 
(spike or two points on one or both antlers), ‘medium’ 
(antlers with 3 or more points; antlers inside ears), or 
large (antlers with ≥ 4 points, antlers outside of ears). 
Snow conditions were excellent, with near 100% 
coverage and cold temperatures (-15 to -25ºC).  
Because transects varied in length, the average 
density (R) of mule deer and white-tailed deer was 
calculated by multiplying the number of animals per 
transect (∑x) by total area (km2) searched (total survey 
strip area [∑z]) (Jolly 1969, as described in Krebs 
2014). Average density (R) was multiplied by the area 
(km2) of the WMU (Z) to determine population 
estimates with 90% confidence intervals. Confidence 
interval width was calculated by multiplying the t 
statistic for the left-tailed inverse of the Student’s t-
distribution, (t0.05,df=n-1) by standard error (SE; without 
replacement) of the abundance estimate where SE=sq 
root variance, and variance=N*(N-n)/(n*(n-
1))*(∑x2+R2*∑z2-2*R*∑xz) with N as the total number 
of possible transects given 100% coverage, and n as 
the number of transects sampled. 
Moose and Elk observations made during the survey 
were also recorded. Elk herds were photographed 
using a Canon EOS R6 Mark II SLR digital camera. 
Obtained photos were subsequently enumerated and 
classified by staff to accurately determine herd sizes 
and composition. Numbers were combined to achieve 
a minimum total count (MTC) survey for WMU 102.  
Moose observations were of insufficient sample size to 
calculate an estimate for the small but persistent 
moose population found in the WMU.

Results 
Mule Deer 
A total of 646 mule deer were observed with an 
average group size of 9 (range 1-24). The estimated 
density was 0.41 mule deer/km2 and the estimated 
abundance was 1,298 individuals (90% CI 956 – 
1640). A total of 637 mule deer were successfully 
classified and the buck:doe:fawn ratio was estimated 
to be 43:100:71. That results in an estimated 2024 
winter mule deer population of 261bucks, 607 does, 
and 430 fawns. Of the 113 mule deer bucks classified, 
31 (27.4%) were classified ‘small’, 49 (43.4%) 
‘medium’, and 33 (29.2%) ‘large’. The 2025 population 
estimate represents a 37% decrease from the last 
aerial ungulate survey population estimate for mule 
deer within WMU 102 (conducted in 2018). The survey 
in 2025 showed similar results in both buck to doe and 
fawn to doe ratios (Table 1). It should be noted that 
several one-antlered bucks were observed indicating 
antler drop was underway, and buck numbers were 
undoubtedly underrepresented in the totals.  
White-tailed Deer 
A total of 166 white-tailed deer were observed with an 
average group size of 15 (range 2-52). The estimated 
density was 0.11 deer/km2 and the estimated 
abundance was 334 individuals (90% CI 192 – 475). 
The timing of the survey did not facilitate classification 
of white-tailed deer as antler drop had occurred and 
differentiation of bucks and does was not possible. 
The 2025 population estimate represents a 67.1% 
decrease when compared to 2018 data. However, 
WMU 116 which borders WMU 102 to the north was 
also flown during the 2025 winter inventory program. 
The white-tailed deer survey in this unit resulted in a 
260% increase in abundance over a survey conducted 
in the previous winter of 2024. Such a dramatic 
increase in abundance cannot be accounted for solely 
by intrinsic growth rate and must indicate significant 
immigration of white-tailed deer into WMU 116 from 
surrounding units. It is therefore likely that white-tailed 
deer from WMU 102 herded up and moved into WMU 
116 due to the relatively severe winter weather that 
occurred in the winter of 2025. Thus, this large 
population decrease is unlikely to reflect the actual 
number of deer in the unit assuming seasonal 
migration back to WMU 102 will occur.  
Elk 
A total of eight elk herds were observed ranging in size 
from two to 409 animals. The combined totals for all 
elk herds observed resulted in a minimum total count 
of 519 animals wintering in WMU 102. The herd was 
comprised of 266 cows, 137 calves, and 116 bulls. 
The bull component of the herd consisted of 24 small, 
55 medium, and 37 large bulls. This results in a herd 
composition of 52 calves and 44 bulls per 100 cows. 
The previous survey conducted in 2018 observed 173 
wintering elk in WMU 102. This herd growth could not 
be explained solely by intrinsic growth rate and must 
indicate significant immigration into the WMU. This 
increase would most likely be explained by an 
incomplete count in 2018. Since the elk herd in this 
area frequently moves across the international border, 
it is likely more elk were wintering in the USA in 2018 
and were not able to be counted.  
Incidental Observations 
A total of seven moose were observed with an 
average group size of 1 (range 1-2). Moose were 
generally confined to brushy areas of river and creek 
valleys and associated coulees as suitable moose 
habitat is generally limited in prairie WMUs.   
An estimated total of 2742 pronghorn were observed 
during the survey. This consisted of 45 herd 
observations with herd sizes ranging from four to an 
estimated 400 head. Other species observed included 
sage-grouse, Sharp-tailed grouse, gray partridge, ring-
necked pheasant, bald eagle, and coyote.
